## Claims

### C-D-01 — Chs. 4–5 as intentional compilation with future vantage
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2834–2837; local 1–4
- **Quote:** “Several signals suggest that chapters 4–5 have been compiled together intentionally to serve a larger rhetorical purpose, specifically to announce both Yahweh’s judgment and restoration of Judah, both of which will take place in the future as seen from the vantage point of the prophet’s lifetime at the end of the eighth century BCE.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Mic 4–5 is a purposeful compilation announcing future judgment and restoration of Judah, viewed from an eighth-century prophetic vantage.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-D-02 — Majority: Persian-period materials; evolving compilation after Mic 1–3
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2835–2837; local 2–4
- **Quote:** “A majority of scholars treat the compilation as consisting of later materials deriving largely from the Persian period. … these chapters did not all enter Micah at the same time, but instead represent an evolving compilation intended to follow Mic 1–3.”
- **Claim (Nogalski reporting scholarship):** Many scholars date much of 4–5 as later (largely Persian) and as layered additions after Mic 1–3.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-D-03 — Four structural groups in Mic 4–5 (formulas)
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2839; local 6
- **Quote:** “These repeating formulas and phrases divide themselves into four recognizable groups: (1) the first group (4:1–7) contains two future-oriented sections (4:1–5, 6–7) that each begin with an eschatological day formula (and it will be in the latter days, on that day), the combination of which (and it will be on that day) also concludes the third and opens the fourth group in Mic 5:10(9); (2) the second group (4:8–5:4[3]) is organized by sound and a change of chronological orientation to the present generation because five of the sayings either begin with (and) you ([wə]ʾattâ in 4:8; 5:2[1]) or with (and) now ([wə]ʿattâ in 4:9, 11; 5:1 [4:14]) …; (3) the third group (5:5–9[4–8]) returns the reader to the future with its repeating use of the word wəhāyâ …; (4) the final group (5:10–15[9–14]) is characterized by the refrain (and I will cut off) …”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Mic 4–5 coheres via four formula groups: eschatological day sayings (4:1–7); you/now sayings (4:8–5:4[3]); future wəhāyâ (5:5–9); “I will cut off” refrain (5:10–15).
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[day-of-the-lord]]

### C-D-04 — Surface unity vs. internal tensions (Babylon vs. Assyria; peace vs. hostility)
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2841; local 8
- **Quote:** “4:10 mentions the exile to Babylon in a way that causes most commentators to recognize that it presupposes the destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BCE. By contrast, the enemy highlighted in 5:5–6(4–5) is the Assyrian kingdom whose capital Nineveh was destroyed in 612 BCE. Additionally, the opening section of this larger block anticipates a time of peace between Judah and the nations, while much of the material that follows anticipates hostile relationships between these entities.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Recurring formulas unify 4–5 while subunits differ (Babylon/587 vs. Assyria; peace vision vs. later hostility); the block has a horizon beyond Micah alone.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-05 — Group 1: two eschatological peace scenarios from different vantage points
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2922; local 89
- **Quote:** “Group 1 consists of two parts (4:1–5, 6–7), both of which begin with an eschatological introduction, and each depicts a scenario of peace among the nations, though from different vantage points. Micah 4:1–5 begins with an eye toward the distant future (in the end of the days). … The second part of group 1 (4:6–7) conveys a promise to gather the afflicted of Yahweh’s own people and turn them into a mighty nation.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 4:1–5 elevates Zion so foreigners seek tōrâ and Yahweh’s justice ends war; 4:6–7 promises gathering of Yahweh’s afflicted into a mighty nation.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]], [[remnant]]

### C-D-06 — 4:1–5 independent unit introducing chs. 4–5; intertextual frame
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2931; local 98
- **Quote:** “Micah 4:1–5 represents an independent unit that has been selected for inclusion in Mic 4–5 to introduce the themes of these chapters in the book. … Micah 4:1–3 contains a close parallel to Isa 2:2–4 … Both texts also reverse the message of Joel 3(4):10. Micah 4:4–5 comments upon 4:1–3 … Relatedly, Mic 4:6–7 anticipates Zeph 3:18–20 with strong allusions to the remnant as the lame and afflicted … that plays a significant role in the Book of the Twelve … As a whole, then, 4:1–5 and 6–7 point the reader outside the book of Micah by recalling texts from the prophetic corpus.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 4:1–5 opens the block with distant-future orientation; 4:1–3 // Isa 2:2–4 reverse Joel 3(4):10; 4:6–7 alludes toward Zeph 3:18–20 / Twelve remnant imagery.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[isaiah]], [[book-of-the-twelve]], [[remnant]]

### C-D-07 — “End of the days”: distant future, not final apocalyptic last judgment
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2933–2934; local 100–101
- **Quote:** “Micah 4:1 marks a dramatic shift in time that in some ways continues for the rest of the book. The opening formula looks forward to the distant future when it begins with the statement, And it will happen in the end of the days. … In prophetic texts, this chronological sense “backside” formula appears in eschatological contexts (e.g., see Jer 23:20; 30:24; Ezek 38:8; Dan 2:28; 10:14; Hos 3:5).”
- **Also (group intro):** raw ≈ 2922; local 89: “It does not, however, imply some final, apocalyptic last judgment scene.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** ʾaḥărît hayyāmîm shifts from eighth-century judgment focus (chs. 1–3) to distant future; not a terminal apocalyptic last-judgment scene.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[day-of-the-lord]]

### C-D-08 — Mic 4:1: Zion elevated politically/spiritually; destination for foreigners
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2935; local 102
- **Quote:** “First, 4:1 promises the elevation of Zion and second, Zion will become a destination for foreigners. … when 4:1 claims that Zion will be raised above all the surrounding hills and be established as the head of the mountains, it is essentially referring to Zion’s political and spiritual significance. … the fact that the promise will not occur until the distant future suggests an awareness on the part of the author that Zion does not yet carry such importance.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** “Mountain of the house of Yahweh” = Mount Zion/temple; elevation is significance, not literal height; delay implies present shortfall of that status.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-09 — Mic vs. Isa 2:2 wording: peoples/nations reverse order; “stream over” vs. “stream to”
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2937; local 104 (cf. text notes local 59–61)
- **Quote:** “Mic 4:1 designates the foreigners as peoples … while the Isaiah parallel merely states that they stream to the mountain. … the fluid movement of the peoples on the mountain comes across more clearly in Mic 4:1. Jerusalem will be teeming with foreigners who have come to learn Yahweh’s tōrâ and submit to Yahweh’s courtroom decisions (see Mic 4:3).”
- **Text note (Nogalski):** “In Micah, they do not merely arrive (stream to the city); rather, their presence looks like a river of people.” (local 59)
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Micah’s preposition/wording portrays a river-like presence of peoples on the mountain more vividly than Isa 2:2’s “stream to”; peoples/nations appear in reverse order across the parallels.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[isaiah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-10 — EXCURSUS: priority of Mic 4:1–3 // Isa 2:2–4 is insoluble
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2940–2941; local 107–108
- **Quote:** “A great deal of attention has been devoted to the study of the virtually identical texts of Mic 4:1–3 and Isa 2:2–4. Much of this attention has focused on the insoluble question of priority, with scholars making sustained arguments for one of three solutions: (1) Micah draws upon Isaiah as its source; (2) Isaiah draws upon Micah as its source; or (3) both draw upon an independent source. Lately … both passages are postexilic additions to the collections in which they appear, making it less likely that either the prophet Micah or Isaiah can be definitively claimed as the author of these texts …”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Priority among three classic options is insoluble; recent postexilic-addition models further undercut prophetic authorship claims for either parallel.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[isaiah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-D-11 — Nogalski’s intertextual method: similar cores; divergent continuations
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2941; local 108
- **Quote:** “Apart from a few minor variations in the order, the two texts display no significant differences of meaning between the two passages. Given that both passages appear at the beginning of new redactional units that change the theme from judgment to promise, neither passage can be said to be clearly more at home in its respective literary context. A close reading of the two passages can, however, demonstrate, despite their similar statements, that the passages diverge significantly from one another in the ways in which the parallel texts continue in their respective contexts. Careful attention will thus be paid to the different endings associated with the parallel verses (Isa 2:4; Mic 4:5) in the discussion of Mic 4:4–5.”
- **Claim (Nogalski’s position):** Do not settle priority; read function by how each book continues after the parallel (esp. Mic 4:4–5 vs. Isa 2:5–6).
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[isaiah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-D-12 — Mic 4:2: voluntary pilgrimage; tôrâ and “word of Yahweh”
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2943–2947; local 110–114
- **Quote:** “this verse not only depicts their trek to Jerusalem as voluntary; it also portrays the nations articulating their desire to submit themselves completely to Yahweh, the God of Jacob. … The verb “to go” (hālak) used to describe the journey of foreign entities into a city would typically signal a military invasion … but the phrasing of this verse implies a different kind of pilgrimage. … They go to Jerusalem because it is the source of both instruction (tôrâ) and the word of Yahweh … The word of Yahweh is associated with prophetic activity while the word instruction (tôrâ) is the word used for the first five books of the Bible, but more importantly, instruction refers to the content of the covenant commitments. … 4:2 presumes that the knowledge that allows one to follow the way of Yahweh derives from teaching and prophecy associated with the temple in Jerusalem.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Nations march as pilgrimage, not invasion; they seek ethical/cultic/prophetic instruction—Torah and Prophets—centered on Jerusalem’s temple.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]], [[isaiah]]

### C-D-13 — Mic 4:3: Yahweh as international judge; voluntary submission vs. Joel 3(4)
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2949; local 116
- **Quote:** “This verse depicts Yahweh as the divine mediator of international disputes whose decisions will eliminate the need for war. … This portrait has some clear affinities with the picture of Yahweh as judge to the nations in Joel 3(4), except that the judicial activity of Yahweh in Joel 3(4) also requires Yahweh’s military intervention with the heavenly host, while the portrait in Mic 4:3 (= Isa 2:4) assumes the nations have voluntarily submitted to Yahweh’s decisions.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Mic 4:3 (= Isa 2:4) ends war via voluntary submission to Yahweh’s verdicts; Joel 3(4) requires heavenly military intervention.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[isaiah]], [[book-of-the-twelve]]

### C-D-14 — Swords into plowshares reverses Joel 3(4):10
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2949–2986; local 116–153
- **Quote:** “Nowhere does this difference manifest itself more clearly than in the reversal of the peaceful promise depicted in Joel 3(4):10: … [Mic:] and they will beat the swords into plow blades, … and their spears into pruning knives. … Nation will not lift sword against nation, and they will no longer learn war. [Joel:] Beat your plow blades into swords … and your pruning knives into spears. … The message of Mic 4:3 (= Isa 2:4) presupposes the peaceful attitude of the nations from 4:1–2, while Joel 3(4):10 (and its larger context) anticipates that Yahweh’s judgment will be implemented by means of futile military measures …”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Mic 4:3 / Isa 2:4 reverse Joel’s plowshares→swords call; Micah/Isaiah assume peaceable nations, Joel a hostile ones.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[isaiah]], [[book-of-the-twelve]]

### C-D-15 — Mic 4:4–5 vs. Isa 2:5–6: parallel cores, opposite continuations
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2989–3011; local 156–178
- **Quote:** “While the parallel passages hardly differ with one another for three verses, their continuations in their respective contexts take very different tracks … Isaiah 2:5–6 admonish Jacob (i.e., Judah) to walk in the light of Yahweh rather than what they have been doing: forsaking that path to follow the divinatory practices of the nations in the present. In other words, the idyllic future described in Isa 2:2–4 … serves as the launching pad for a critique against Yahweh’s own people. By contrast, the continuation of the parallel in Micah (4:4–5) maintains the focus on the future as a time of peace for both Judah and the nations, even though it steps back from the idea of the nations’ radical submission to Yahweh as depicted in Mic 4:1–3.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** After the shared peace oracle, Isaiah pivots to present critique of Jacob; Micah extends future peace for Judah and nations while qualifying religious conversion of the nations.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[isaiah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-D-16 — Mic 4:4: vine and fig tree; traditional fertility/security formula
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3013; local 180
- **Quote:** “Micah 4:4 picks up traditional language about the fertility of the land to portray the time of Yahweh’s peace (4:3) as both a time when the land will produce its fruit and when the inhabitants can enjoy that produce without fear of enemy attack. … A person owns land; the land produces enough to survive; the land is not threatened. … it ends with a citation formula: for the mouth of Yahweh Sabaoth has spoken.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 4:4 uses traditional vine/fig-tree language for secure prosperity under Yahweh’s spoken guarantee.
- **Related:** [[micah]]

### C-D-17 — Mic 4:5 qualifies 4:1–3: nations keep their gods; “we” walk with Yahweh
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3013; local 180 (cf. translation local 47; LXX note local 79)
- **Quote:** “Micah 4:5 claims emphatically that the nations who have come to Jerusalem will not become religious converts as 4:2 would suggest. Rather, the nations will worship their own deities (i.e., all the peoples will walk in the name of their own god). Conversely, 4:5 states just as emphatically that the relationship between Yahweh and the people has changed in the future (4:1, 6) from what was described in Mic 1–3. … Mic 4:1–5 anticipates a time of peace in the distant future … when the nations voluntarily submit to Yahweh’s judgment and leave the land in peace. In so doing, 4:1–5 interprets the coming judgment announced in 3:12 as a period of punishment that has an end.”
- **Text note:** “The LXX changes this verse to avoid any implications of henotheism. … the LXX removes any doubt that other gods could exist.” (local 79)
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 4:5 (possibly secondary gloss or redactional transition) denies full conversion of the nations while affirming Israel’s perpetual walk with Yahweh; 3:12 judgment is thus time-bounded.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-18 — 4:6–7 same “day” as 4:1–5; fills fate-of-the-judged gap
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3024–3025; local 191–192
- **Quote:** “Specifically, the formula presumes an antecedent reference to a coming time. Logically, the phrase on that day places the action that follows in the same time as that which has preceded. In the case of Mic 4:6, this formula means that the action described in 4:6–7 occurs at the same time as the material in 4:1–5 (at least for the redactor who has brought this material together). … Micah 1–3 culminates in the pronouncement of Jerusalem’s destruction, but Mic 4:1–5 does not address the fate of those who experience that judgment. Micah 4:6–7 addresses this missing piece with a divine speech announcing Yahweh’s decision to gather the remnant back in Jerusalem into perpetuity.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** “On that day” synchronizes 4:6–7 with 4:1–5 for the redactor; 4:6–7 supplies remnant restoration after 3:12’s destruction.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[remnant]], [[jerusalem]], [[day-of-the-lord]]

### C-D-19 — Lame / banished / afflicted: metaphors for left-behind and exiled after 587
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3030–3032; local 197–199
- **Quote:** “The feminine singular noun “the lame” and the feminine singular participle “the one banished” imply one group that will be wounded and another group that will be expelled (from Jerusalem). The feminine singular forms here function as collective nouns. … Since chapters 4–5 as a whole anticipate the destruction of Jerusalem in 587, identifying these two distinct groups likely means these words function as poetic metaphors for those left behind after Jerusalem’s destruction (the lame) and those who were exiled to Babylon (the one banished). … Since Yahweh is the speaker, Yahweh thus claims credit for the coming judgment on Jerusalem …”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 4:6’s collectives = post-587 survivors vs. Babylonian exiles; Yahweh owns the affliction (rʿʿ hiphil).
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[remnant]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-20 — Two-step restoration: gather then make remnant / mighty nation; Yahweh reigns on Zion
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3034; local 201 (cf. translation local 49–53)
- **Quote:** “The result is a two-step process: I will gather the lame (4:6) and make (them) into a remnant. … Yahweh will first gather (4:6) those who have been expelled and (then) make them into … a mighty nation.”
- **Translation:** “And Yahweh will reign over them on Mount Zion from now into perpetuity.” (local 53)
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 4:6–7: gather → constitute remnant / mighty nation; Yahweh (not a human king alone) reigns forever on Zion.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[remnant]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-21 — Group B (4:8–5:4[3]): five you/now sayings; sound-play frame
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3141–3142; local 308–309
- **Quote:** “The second group of texts in Mic 4–5 consists of a series of five sayings in 4:8–5:4(3). These five units are: 4:8, 9–10, 11–13; 5:1 (4:14); and 5:2–4(1–3). These sayings are introduced by either and you (wəʾattâ in 4:8; 5:2[1]) or now (ʿattâ in 4:9, 5:1 [4:14] and wəʿattâ in 4:11). … Even though spelled differently, you and now sound similar in Hebrew. … The you sayings occupy the outer part of the frame … while the triple use of now in the internal portions of this group emphatically creates a sense of urgency.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Five sayings cohere by ʾattâ / ʿattâ sound; outer “you” frame + inner “now” urgency; arrangement progresses the fate of Judah/Zion.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-22 — Mic 4:8: “you” = Mount Zion (tower of the flock / hill of Lady Zion); former dominion returns
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3148–3162; local 315–329
- **Quote:** “Syntactically, 4:8 addresses a masculine-singular entity directly, but the metaphorical language combined with an appositional phrase equating tower of the flock and the hill of Lady Zion technically means that Mount Zion constitutes the most likely conceptual entity addressed by this verse. … 4:8 picks up both the addressee of Mount Zion (4:1, 2, 7) and the theme of the restoration of the kingdom (4:7) from the preceding unit, making it highly likely that someone composed 4:8 for its context as an artistically constructed bridge to the three now sayings that follow …”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 4:8 is an artful bridge: Mount Zion addressed as “you”; promise of former dominion/kingdom to Lady Jerusalem; composed for its place after 4:1–7.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-23 — “Tower of the flock”: metaphorical Jerusalem height, not primarily Bethlehem town
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3164–3169; local 331–336
- **Quote:** “The phrase tower of the flock has created interpretive difficulties since the phrase in Hebrew is also associated with something near Bethlehem in the Jacob story (Gen 35:19–21) … The recognition of this language as metaphorical makes far better sense of the phrase, even if it is also a play on words to place-names associated with Bethlehem. The parallel of the mountain and the hill refers to the entire elevated portion of Jerusalem. This portion of Jerusalem included the king’s house and the temple.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Prefer metaphorical reading of migdal-ʿēder for Jerusalem’s elevated royal/temple area; possible wordplay with Bethlehem-adjacent Gen 35 tradition.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-24 — 4:8 and Davidic restoration hopes (LXX “from Babylon”; Zerubbabel/Hag parallel)
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3171; local 338
- **Quote:** “The fact that the LXX includes the phrase “from Babylon” shows that either the translator or the source text saw this verse as a prophecy of Jerusalem’s destruction in 587 BCE. Critical scholarship that sees Mic 4–5 as a postexilic composition sees this statement as part of the redaction of Micah when the idea of a restoration of the Davidic kingdom might still have been envisioned. In Hag 2:20–23, Yahweh seems to express similar ideas concerning Zerubbabel … This statement about Zerubbabel reverses the oracle in Jer 22:24–30 …”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 4:8’s dominion promise read in postexilic redaction as restored kingdom hope; reception links to 587 and Davidic restoration discourse (Hag vs. Jer 22).
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-25 — 4:9–10: “now” shifts to Lady Zion’s distress; exile to Babylon; Yahweh still king
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3179–3188; local 346–355
- **Quote:** “Micah 4:9 begins a series of three small units (4:9–10, 11–13, 5:1 [4:14]) that all begin with now … and that all address Lady Zion. … 4:10 refers explicitly to the events of 587 and Jerusalem’s exile: you will go to Babylon. Clearly, 4:10 forces the reader to recognize that the now in 4:9 refers to the deportation and/or destruction of Jerusalem at the beginning of the sixth century BCE. … Her king is still with her, and her counselor has not perished. She will endure punishment, but she will be redeemed by Yahweh. Jerusalem does not need a human king because Yahweh functions as king.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 4:9’s rhetorical questions are answered by 4:10: Babylon exile affirmed; deliverance/redemption “there” proves Yahweh remains Zion’s king/counselor.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-26 — Birth-pangs imagery and bat ṣiyyôn as “Lady Zion”
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3189–3201; local 356–368 (translation local 220–232; note local 278)
- **Quote:** “Writhe [2fs], and burst forth [2fs], Lady Zion … For now, you [2fs] will go forth from a village, And you [2fs] will dwell in a field.” / “Translators often translate the Hebrew phrase bat șîōn literally as “Daughter of Zion,” but this translation potentially miscommunicates the concept of bat when used with cities in West Semitic contexts. … When biblical writers borrow the term … when Zion is personified as Jerusalem, she and her children (the inhabitants of Jerusalem) have a special relationship with Yahweh.”
- **Frontmatter note:** “Literally, the term bat ṣiyyôn means “Daughter Zion” or “Daughter of Zion,” but in prophetic literature, this term is a title that plays off Western Semitic traditions of personified cities. The term Lady Zion thus communicates this titular function.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Birth-pangs metaphors frame exile path (village→field→Babylon); “Lady Zion” better captures city-personification than bare “Daughter of Zion.”
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-27 — 4:11–13: nations taunt Zion; Yahweh’s plans; threshing-floor judgment
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3206–3216; local 373–383
- **Quote:** “The second now saying introduces a three-verse unit (4:11–13) … many nations will seek to take advantage of Jerusalem’s punishment. … The speech they are quoted as saying (Let her be defiled, and let our eyes gaze on Zion) draws upon language that typifies poetic descriptions of the city’s destruction. The imagery carries subtle but clear sexual overtones … Micah 4:12 contrasts the nations’ enjoyment of Zion’s distress (4:11) with an ominous statement regarding the fate of the nations … The verse opens with a statement that could well be an allusion to Jer 29:11 … In response, Yahweh will gather those nations like grain from the threshing floor (4:12) where they will be stomped by a rampaging Lady Zion …”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Second “now” unit: opportunistic nations taunt defiled Zion; they miss Yahweh’s plans; gathered like grain for crushing judgment.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-28 — Jer 29:11 parallel instructive but different restoration focus
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3210–3215; local 377–382
- **Quote:** “Both passages presuppose an exile to Babylon (Jer 29:10; Mic 4:10) … Yet both passages also presuppose that these events represent only one piece of larger plans of (maḥăšābôt) restoration that Yahweh intends (Jer 29:11; Mic 4:12). … The Jeremiah text presupposes the need for the people to demonstrate repentance by seeking Yahweh, and the restoration described in the passage speaks primarily about a return to the land … By contrast, Mic 4:11–13 delivers a promise to Lady Zion … The plans of Yahweh in the Micah context do not focus upon the return of the inhabitants. Rather, they focus upon the punishment of those nations who have taken advantage of Zion’s calamity.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Shared “plans” language with Jer 29, but Micah’s restoration accent is retributive action via Zion against nations, not primarily return-from-exile instruction to deportees.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-29 — 4:13: Lady Zion as aggressive warrior (iron horn, copper hooves)
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3218–3219; local 385–386
- **Quote:** “The guiding metaphor of the verse depicts Lady Zion as a rampaging bull, designed for war with metal horns and feet. … Micah 4:13 presents Lady Zion as an aggressive, powerful warrior whose actions will crush the nations and fill the coffers of Yahweh, and that image differs from the imagery as it more typically appears, where the city personified is condemned as a harlot … portrayed as a grieving mother … or as the more or less passive recipient of Yahweh’s actions … In Mic 4:13, by contrast, Yahweh acts toward Zion so that she crushes the nations with her metal hooves.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Unusual Lady Zion tradition: Zion as active warrior instrument of Yahweh’s retribution and devotion of booty, not passive restored city.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-30 — 5:1 (4:14): “Now, muster yourself, Lady Muster”; siege; strike judge on the cheek
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3231–3233; local 398–400
- **Quote:** “This saying (5:1 [4:14]) begins with a feminine singular imperative delivered to Lady Zion … The exhortation calls for her to muster herself … the title by which Lady Zion is addressed changes in 5:1 (4:14) to Lady Muster … In 5:1 (4:14), she is exhorted … to rally her troops because a siege is about to begin against us … the attackers strike the judge of Israel on the cheek (5:1b). … it seems probable that the judge of Israel refers figuratively to the king of Judah. … Most, therefore, treat the blow as nonlethal.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Fourth “now” saying: wordplay muster/Lady Muster; siege setting; cheek-strike = humiliation of Judah’s king, not necessarily death.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-D-31 — Multivalent siege: 701 and/or 587; literary “now” for later readers
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3234–3240; local 401–407
- **Quote:** “Some commentators believe that the “slap” alludes to Sennacherib’s attack of Hezekiah in the siege of 701 … Other commentators see 5:1 (4:14) as a reference to the events of 587 BCE because the evidence suggests chapters 4–5 were added to Micah after Jerusalem’s destruction in 587 BCE. … The image need not be formulated to refer exclusively to Jerusalem’s destruction in 587 BCE or to the events of 701 BCE, because one thing is sure: both events resulted in a dramatic change in the power structure of Judah and Jerusalem that reduced the power of the Judean monarch. … This multivalent interpretation presupposes that the now statements can refer to the “now” of the literary setting in the time of Hezekiah (cf. Mic 1:1). Recognizing this multivalence, however, means that these now statements can also force the original readers to consider their own time … (which for most scholars would be sometime during the Persian period).”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** 5:1’s siege/humiliation is multivalent (Assyrian Hezekiah / Babylonian kings / Persian-period readers); “now” works as literary and reader-time address—promise and shame over lost native kingship.
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-D-32 — Text-critical: Mic 4:1–5 apparatus highlights (LXX henotheism; house of Yahweh)
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2888–2912; local 55–79
- **Quote:** “House is not present in the LXX. … the fact that Isa 2:2 has the same phrase in the Hebrew text suggests the MT is original. … The LXX changes this verse [4:5] to avoid any implications of henotheism. Where the MT has all the peoples will walk, each in the name of its own god, the LXX changes it to “all the peoples will walk, each in its own way.” … the change was motivated by theological concerns related to monotheism.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** MT “house of Yahweh” preferred (// Isa); LXX of 4:5 theologically revises away other-gods language; other minor Greek variants noted (swords vocabulary; “afflicted” vs. “rejected”).
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[isaiah]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-D-34 — LXX 4:6–7 theological softening; feminine participles anticipate Lady Zion
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2914–2920; local 81–87
- **Quote:** “the LXX reading softens the idea that God causes evil. … The use of the feminine participle probably anticipates the address of Lady Zion that begins in 4:8.”

### C-D-35 — “On that day” = future historical intervention, not single end-time judgment
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 3028; local 195
- **Quote:** “By having Yahweh state that it will happen on that day, the reader associates the coming action with the eschatological future, but one should not think of this as single final judgment at the end of time. Rather, the formula on that day refers to a time in the future when Yahweh will intervene in human history.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Day formula marks future divine intervention in history, not a unique terminal judgment event.
- **Related:** [[day-of-the-lord]], [[micah]]

### C-D-36 — Peace vision (4:1–5) vs. later hostility within same block
- **Locus:** raw ≈ 2841; local 8 (cf. 4:11–13 claims)
- **Quote:** “the opening section of this larger block anticipates a time of peace between Judah and the nations, while much of the material that follows anticipates hostile relationships between these entities. Understanding how to account for both the unifying elements and the different messages of the subunits within Mic 4–5 requires that the reader search for literary cues from the text, but also recognize that these chapters have a broader literary horizon than simply the book of Micah.”
- **Claim (Nogalski):** Tension between opening peace vision and subsequent hostile nation-Judah relations is intentional for literary/redactional reading, with horizon beyond Micah alone (Twelve/prophetic corpus).
- **Related:** [[micah]], [[book-of-the-twelve]]
